facts.state_of_play: Nearly a week after the Nov. 3 midterms, in which Democrats won both houses of Congress, Trump questioned the results without evidence on Truth Social Monday, reviving voting-machine claims after saying he accepted the outcome and might deal with Democrats. The administration asked the Supreme Court to make California set aside about 20,000 mail-in ballots, and DOJ is appealing dismissal of an Alaska Senate election suit. Officials are also leaving: Civil Division head Brett Shumate resigned Monday, and WH deputy chief of staff Richard Walters resigned Friday, amid a wave of post-midterm departures as Stephen Miller becomes chief of staff. Trump also ordered DOJ on Saturday to investigate members of Congress who proposed impeaching AG Blanche. Blanche signaled on CNN Sunday that Democrats could be investigated, and Sen. Elissa Slotkin's lawyer warned him not to obey Trump's demand to investigate her. Congressional Republicans are in turmoil after losing at least 30 House seats: House and Senate GOP leadership elections are set for Tuesday. Ron Johnson and four allies want the Senate vote delayed, targeting John Thune, while John Barrasso is seeking another term as whip. The party turmoil extends to the RNC: Trump is reportedly threatening to cut off the committee unless it reelects his pick, chair Joe Gruters, after co-chair KC Crosbie launched a challenge. Separately, Trump on Monday blamed old technology and the Biden administration for last week's nationwide grounding of all planes.

facts.state_of_play: Stephen Miller took over as White House chief of staff on Monday, replacing Susie Wiles, after Republicans lost the House and Senate in the midterms. Trump, after initially signaling acceptance, has questioned the early vote numbers and ballot machines, and admitted deportation policy was 'too tough'. Jeffries, poised to be Speaker, says Democrats will focus on affordability and corruption. Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO after 33 years amid allegations of two affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, but Nvidia's board has now reinstated him as CEO less than two weeks after his ousting, reversing earlier reports that it was not considering this. Stocks rallied sharply Monday: the S&P 500 rose nearly 5% and the Dow gained over 1,500 points after a brutal week in which the Nasdaq fell 10%. Lawmakers of both parties reacted with anger and skepticism and still expect Huang to answer questions on Capitol Hill next week. Trump has arrived in China for the APEC summit in Shenzhen, with a historic first trilateral meeting with Xi and Putin plus a Thursday one-on-one with Putin on Ukraine and security guarantees. The agenda reportedly includes nuclear arms limits, with New START expired and China's arsenal above 600 warheads. A US-North Korea meeting with Kim Jong Un is uncertain, and Kim's presence is up to Xi. The administration is moving forward with an interim rule requiring licenses to export AI chips if they may provide compute to China or other restricted countries. A Friday FAA nationwide ground stop of over four hours disrupted over a million passengers; Trump blames old equipment, and Mullin says no one will be fired. Michigan Democrats remain split over Haley Stevens endorsing Mike Rogers.

facts.state_of_play: Ukraine has struck the Kerch (Crimea) bridge repeatedly: two attacks destroyed a road section, and a third attack this week was reported Wednesday by a Russian-installed governor, with damage assessment underway. Ukraine reportedly used homegrown relay drones to bypass Starlink limits. AI-generated fake videos of a collapsed bridge are circulating. The strikes came amid a record drone barrage (Moscow cites 1,336 drones in one barrage; BBC reports over 2,000 in a day). Ukrainian and Russian alert apps were hacked hours apart, sending false warnings; neither government has said who is responsible, and Russia is restoring its app. Russian spies accuse Ukraine of sabotaging drone pilots' goggles. The EU sanctioned the Wildberries founder.

facts.state_of_play: Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO and president on Monday, effective immediately, less than two weeks after he resigned on Nov. 12 amid reports of multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a woman suspected of spying for China, and reportedly one with a direct report. NYT reports US intelligence tracked her contacts with China's Ministry of State Security. The US is probing Alice Huang and Singapore-based Megaspeed, the firm at the heart of the chip case. Commerce is set to add Megaspeed to the trade blacklist, requiring a license for US chip sales to it. Trump and Vance reportedly intervened. Trump told CNBC he spoke to the board and to Xi about Huang, that Huang did nothing wrong, and that the board sought national security assurances. He cited the attorney general and urged Nvidia to continue its export-control investigation. The board cited input from senior levels of government, and a probe into Huang's conduct is reportedly ongoing. Interim CEO Kress and senior management were not consulted. Stock rose over 30%, adding about $1 trillion in value. Lawmakers in both parties criticize the move. Jeffries wants export controls added to the defense policy bill.
